items.content:
Nobody wakes up one day and decides: "I want a career in supply chain."
At least no one I know ...

(including me)

I didn't choose this industry. I ended up in my family's business because they needed help, and I needed a paycheck. 

That was the whole plan. There was no 'this is my calling' moment.

Decades later, that after-school job became a career I never saw coming - and eventually, a company I built from nothing.

Here's what nobody tells you about accidental careers:
✔️ You don't need a grand plan to build real expertise
 ✔️ Resilience beats a perfect path, every time
 ✔️ The self-awareness to ask "what do I need to learn next" matters more than the job title you started with

There's no playbook for going from "I took this job because I needed one" to "I'm actually good at this, and I'm not leaving."

You just build it as you go.

I recently talked about this with Chris Hamley, CEO of Brecham Group, on the Let's Talk Supply Chain pod. 

He's spent 37 years in this industry, and started out loading trucks at UPS.

And now I'm curious ... what's one skill or career path you never planned on that ended up defining you?

items.content:
I'm a frequent flyer, so I have a whole system down.

Small bag in the overhead. Laptop in front of me. Headphones on before we take off. And at least a few episodes of Love Island UK downloaded. 
 
What I never think about is what's happening under my feet ...
 
Because underneath the floor of that plane is an entire second operation running: freight, mail, sometimes even parts of a factory.

Most of us never think about it once. Why would we?!
 
That operation essentially runs on its own version of what we deal with at the gate (except it's not $45 to check a bag). 

It's fuel surcharges and accessorial fees that can make or break a shipper's margins overnight.
 
This is what I recently talked about with Marco Ferrara from Delta Air Lines and Ed Burek from SmartKargo.

I asked them: when did surcharges stop being about the actual cost ... and start being a 'lever' companies pull whenever they want more revenue?
 
The answer: "A lot of businesses are built on surcharges. It's become a mechanism to dial up your revenue."
 
Once you see the pattern, you can't unsee it. Because it's not just airlines. 

It's SaaS pricing. Service fees. "Convenience" charges. Almost every industry has a version of the $45 checked bag fee ...
 
Surcharges used to track real costs. Now, they're a revenue driver. And customers (like you and me) can tell the difference, even when we can't name it
 
---

I had fun recording this episode with Marco and Ed at Home Delivery World. 

You can check out our full conversation on YouTube or wherever you listen to podcasts: https://lnkd.in/eGsddGXH

items.content:
You'll never out-spend Amazon. But you can absolutely out-care them.

Here's why:
Nobody remembers the checkout page. 
They remember the box on their doorstep. 

Whether it showed up when it was supposed to. Whether the brand felt like it cared ... or like it moved on to the next sale the second you paid.

That moment (the one most companies treat as an afterthought) is the part your customer actually feels.

My conversation with Itamar Zur, CEO and Co-Founder of Veho, reminded me of something I've believed for years: you don't beat the retail giants by copying them.

So if you sell anything online, here are 3 things worth remembering:
📦 Speed matters, but feeling seen matters more
📦 "Efficient" and "memorable" aren't the same thing
📦 The moment someone gets what they ordered is the moment they decide if they're coming back

What's a delivery experience that actually made you loyal to a brand?

items.content:
Doesn't it seem like some teams are constantly putting out fires (while others barely seem to have them)?

I used to think that came down to luck or budget. Turns out it's neither ...

The teams that appear "calm" still have problems. They just catch them early enough to still be able to fix them.

That's what I recently talked about with David Gal, VP of Product & Engineering at Samsara.

I had an opportunity to interview him in person at the Samsara Beyond conference, which is always my favorite. You can actually feel how much someone loves the thing they've built when you speak with them face to face.

We got into something that sounds technical but really isn't. Most tracking gives you a scan when a shipment leaves, a scan when it arrives, and a whole lot of nothing in between. 

So when something goes sideways (a delay, a theft, etc.), you're usually the last to know - and at that point, the problem becomes much harder to fix.

If you move product for a living, you're going to want to remember this one thing David said:

👉🏻 You don't need to track everything the same way 👈🏻

It's a way smarter investment when you match the level of visibility to what's **actually** at risk.

When you do that, you stop reacting to every little problem and start anticipating them.

Which honestly, isn't a supply chain skill ... it's a leadership one that every industry could benefit from.

📌 Worth saving for the next time you're deciding where to spend and where to hold back.

items.content:
Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce got married last Friday, and while everyone was wondering about her dress, my supply chain brain went straight to the loading dock 😅

The wedding lasted one night.
But the load-in took a week.

We saw countless trucks at Madison Square Garden. Crates wrapped in plastic. Handwritten labels on boxes. Streets closed. 

Crews carrying in rigging, lighting, and apparently an entire garden - every piece under packing blankets so nobody outside knew what was happening inside.

By Friday night, you couldn't see any of it. A thousand guests walked into a secret garden.

But that's the whole job, isn't it?

➡️ Somebody figured out how to build all of that in an arena with other events on the calendar
➡️ Somebody sourced flowers at a volume that doesn't exist on a normal week
➡️ Somebody stood on a sidewalk at 5AM directing trucks nobody will ever thank them for

Listen, I've spent almost twenty years in supply chain and logistics. The pattern never changes. 

When it goes right, it looks like it was always going to ... but when it goes wrong, suddenly everyone learns your name.

The people who make the impossible look effortless are almost never the ones in the photos.

items.content:
Someone on your team is probably censoring themselves right now.
What they say in a meeting. What they wear to the office (or on a Zoom call). 

All quietly adjusted to fit what your workplace rewards.

That's called "code-switching."

It means changing how you show up (speech, dress, mannerisms, body language) so you'll be more accepted or taken more seriously. 

And for a lot of people, especially anyone who's ever felt "othered" at work, it isn't occasional. 

It's every single day.

I'll be honest, I didn't know much about code-switching until it came up on the Blended pod. And once I understood it, I couldn't unsee it.

Leah McClure, Jeffrey Roe, and Dr. Lola Adeyemo joined me to talk about what it actually costs. 

One of them called it "a backpack of rocks." You carry it all day, and after a while you stop noticing the weight.

As a CEO, here's what I keep coming back to:
If people feel they have to code-switch to belong, something in the environment taught them that.

Which means WE built it ... and WE can also change it.

So, what does this look like for leaders?

✔️ Put the unwritten rules in writing - stop making people guess what "professional" means here
✔️ Reward the work itself, not how polished someone looks doing it
✔️ Go first - when a leader shows up fully themselves, everyone else gets permission to

Our full convo is available wherever you listen to podcasts.

I hope you give it a listen or share this with someone who's building a team where people don't have to shrink to fit.

A simple framework for creating a learning culture at work: "Empower. Celebrate. Catch."

That's what Keith Bilous taught us on the latest Blended Pledge episode. Let me break it down for you.

✅ Empower = Create real space for people to try new things. Don't just tell them, "you're allowed to." 

✅ Celebrate = When someone gets it right, say so (out loud)! Make it a moment they'll actually remember. 

✅ Catch = Be there when someone fails (because they will). And when they know they aren't alone, they'll feel safe enough to try again.

Listen, the first two are manageable. Most of us leaders can empower and celebrate our team.

But the "catch?" That's where it gets REAL.

Because building a team that actually knows how to learn means making failure the beginning of the conversation ... not the end of it.

We got into all of this and a lot more with Keith, Opal Portis, Ellin Sidell, PMP, ACC, and Lauren Guidry.

Our entire conversation was about why learning culture matters so much right now, what gets in the way of building one, and what it actually looks like when a team gets it right.

I learned a lot from this group. As a CEO, it's the kind of conversation I didn't know I needed - and if you're in any kind of leadership role, I think it'll resonate with you too.

---

Which of these three does your team struggle with most?

items.content:
In my early 20s, I was part of a sting operation.

Not a metaphor. ACTUAL authorities. ACTUAL criminals. One of them had a knife.

I was working at a warehouse when a shipment of drugs came through - hidden in cargo. 

The police set things up. I was there when the men came back with the customs stamp at the back of the dock. They were taken into custody.

After that, their colleagues (truck drivers who knew what had happened) would walk past me in the warehouse and say, "We know what you did."

Customs later asked me to testify at trial. The guys disappeared before the date, so I never had to go.

But I've never forgotten what that felt like.

Crime in supply chain isn't theoretical. It never was.

I was talking to Robert Strenk at SecurSpace recently, and he said something that stopped me:

"Criminals are staying a step ahead, and AI accelerates that."

That's not a line you can ignore.

But here's the part that gave me hope ... Bobby also said:
"We're at a point where people understand the importance of working together to solve the problem."

THAT shift - from competitive silence to collective action - is what actually moves the needle.

The leaders I keep seeing pull ahead aren't protecting their playbooks. They're sharing them.

items.content:
For 15 years, I didn't know what was happening to my body.

Doctors told me to eat less. Run more.
I was playing softball five nights a week, so that wasn't exactly the problem.

So I covered my legs. Stopped wearing dresses. And stopped going back.

That decision cost me years.

Eventually, I learned I had lipedema - a chronic condition that affects 11% of women and almost no one has heard of.

Since then: two surgeries, full-body compression suits, and more complicated feelings about my body than I can count.

But the part I can't get over? I didn't have the self-worth to keep pushing back. 

And that silence made everything harder.

I write about this in my memoir, but the lesson I keep coming back to is bigger than one condition:

The way we advocate for ourselves (or don't) has real consequences.

Not just in business. In our own health. In our own lives.

Self-worth isn't a 'soft skill.' It's what keeps you in the room when every room is telling you to leave.

June is #LipedemaAwarenessMonth.

If you've been told "just lose weight" when something still feels wrong - please, keep going! You're not imagining it.

🔁 Share this with someone who needs to hear it.

The person responsible for the infrastructure that made 2-day Prime delivery possible at scale. He left in 2018 and built Shipium, a platform that processes over 400 million shipments using real-time, carrier-agnostic routing decisions.

His whole platform is the dynamic model the trucking industry refuses to adopt for surcharges. We are getting into it.
